item.title: ‘Apologies’ are no longer enough: public lashes out at Tonga Power...

item.content:encoded:
Fresh public complaints and outrage have erupted over continuing electricity outages across Tongatapu, as Tonga Power Limited (TPL) extends load shedding to more communities barely a month after commissioning two new generators intended to improve the island’s unreliable power supply.

Households and businesses are again facing disruptions, with consumers questioning why electricity shortages persist despite recent investment in additional generation capacity.

In a public advisory dated November 19, Tonga Power confirmed that a problem with one of its diesel generators had reduced available electricity capacity, forcing controlled outages to prevent a wider system blackout.

The company subsequently announced that more communities had been added to the load-shedding programme as demand continued to exceed available supply.

“Electricity demand continues to exceed the power currently available, so load shedding must be extended to more areas,” TPL said.

The company apologised for the disruption and short notice but warned that outages would not follow fixed schedules. Their timing would depend on electricity demand and the availability of solar and wind generation.

New generators fail to end electricity shortages

The latest problems come just weeks after Tonga Power commissioned two Cummins QSK60 generators at Popua Power Station on October 17, adding 3.52 megawatts to Tongatapu’s generation capacity.

The additional generators were intended to strengthen supply reliability during periods of high demand, scheduled maintenance and unexpected equipment failures.

However, the return of load shedding has raised questions about whether the island has sufficient operating capacity and backup generation to maintain reliable electricity services.

TPL has not identified which generator developed the latest fault or indicated whether either of the newly commissioned units is affected.

The November 19 advisory identified daytime outages affecting parts of Tofoa, Fasi, Pili, Fuaʻamotu, Lavengatonga, Maʻufanga, Haʻamoko, Vaini and Makeke.

Nighttime interruptions were also announced for communities including Houmakelikao, Fangaloto, ʻUmusi, Patangata, Tokomololo, Kalaʻau, Haʻatafu, Pea, Liahona and Popua.

Further areas were subsequently added, with TPL acknowledging that the expansion had been announced at short notice.

The absence of fixed outage times has compounded uncertainty for households and businesses attempting to plan their daily activities.

Angry consumers lash out at Tonga Power board and government

Public frustration has increasingly turned towards Tonga Power’s board of directors, with some angry commenters using profanity to condemn its leadership over the continuing electricity outages.

Others questioned how the company could continue experiencing longstanding generation problems despite collecting electricity payments from households and businesses for years.

They argued that revenue from consumers should have provided sufficient resources to maintain equipment, repair faulty generators and prevent the repeated disruptions that have affected communities across Tongatapu.

The criticism also extended to the Tongan Government, with some commenters accusing Cabinet ministers of prioritising frequent overseas travel while residents struggled with serious problems at home.

They questioned why ministers appeared able to undertake repeated international trips while essential public services, including electricity, remained unreliable.

The complaints reflected growing dissatisfaction not only with the outages themselves but also with the accountability of those responsible for managing the country’s electricity infrastructure.

For many consumers, Tonga Power’s latest apology appeared to offer little reassurance after years of recurring blackouts.

The latest public outrage follows months of similar complaints over recurring electricity failures.

Kaniva Tonga News reported in March and April that residents had criticised repeated blackouts, generator failures and damaged overhead power lines.

Some appealed directly to Prime Minister Lord Fakafanua and Cabinet ministers after prolonged outages disrupted village water pumps and left households without running water.

The problems also affected essential public services. In April, the Ministry of Justice confirmed that electricity interruptions had temporarily disabled its civil registry system, preventing the issuance of birth, death and marriage certificates.

These earlier disruptions highlight the longstanding nature of Tonga’s electricity problems, which have persisted despite efforts to improve generation capacity.

While TPL maintains that controlled outages are necessary to prevent a complete system blackout, the latest disruptions have left consumers questioning when reliable electricity services will be restored.

The company has not announced when the current load-shedding programme will end.

item.title: Vava’u bank manager allegedly flees to Fiji, then NZ amid missing...

item.content:encoded:
Allegations that up to TOP$700,000 is missing from Tonga Development Bank’s (TDB) Vavaʻu branch have emerged alongside unverified reports that its manager left Tonga for Fiji before travelling to New Zealand, following confirmation of a police investigation.

The latest developments come against a troubled history of financial and governance controversies at TDB, including a previous embezzlement conviction at the same branch, regulatory intervention by the National Reserve Bank of Tonga (NRBT), disputed lending arrangements and court proceedings involving its former leadership.

Following concerns raised in Parliament about the government-backed financial institution, an Asian Development Bank (ADB) assessment was commissioned in 2025, resulting in recommendations for reforms to strengthen the bank’s governance, financial management and regulatory compliance.

In a statement issued on 16 November 2026, TDB confirmed that a serious matter involving its Vavaʻu branch had been referred to Tonga Police but did not disclose the alleged financial discrepancies or identify any employees suspected of involvement. TDB said it could not disclose further details while police investigations were ongoing but assured customers that arrangements were in place to maintain banking services in Vavaʻu.

Kaniva Tonga News has sought clarification from TDB regarding further allegations that have emerged since the initial revelations.

The bank has been asked whether the discrepancies were discovered during an internal audit conducted by an auditor from its Tongatapu headquarters and whether the branch manager left during the audit before travelling to Fiji and New Zealand.

Further questions concern allegations that funds were transferred into the manager’s personal Bank South Pacific (BSP) account, other branch employees were placed on temporary leave, and whether the manager has been implicated in the alleged disappearance of funds.

Previous Vavaʻu embezzlement uncovered after LDS Church inquiry

The latest investigation follows an earlier embezzlement case at the same branch, uncovered after a United States-based official of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS) questioned missing church deposits.

According to an April 2024 Supreme Court judgment, Duran Ormond, an LDS Church manager based in Utah, contacted TDB headquarters in November 2022 after several tithing deposits made at the Vavaʻu branch failed to appear in the Church’s account.

The initial discrepancies involved four deposits totalling TOP$9,950.40 from congregations at Haʻalaufuli, Taʻanea and Holeva.

Unable to locate copies of the deposit receipts, TDB obtained replacements from the Church and dispatched an internal auditor, Samiu Fifita, from Tongatapu.

The investigation uncovered additional irregularities, including customer deposit receipts found in a teller’s locked cabinet without corresponding cash.

Former teller ʻEva ʻAilolo, also known as ʻEva ʻi Pomana Tauʻese, was subsequently convicted of embezzling TOP$72,857.60 and sentenced to nine months’ imprisonment in April 2024.

Reserve Bank intervention and leadership controversy

In May 2024, the NRBT issued supervisory directives against TDB’s then chief executive, ʻEmeline Tuita, and board chairman Penisimani Vea, citing concerns about unsafe and unsound banking practices.

The regulator sought their removal, prompting a legal challenge by TDB.

In September 2024, the Supreme Court granted interim relief allowing the two officials to remain in their positions pending further proceedings, while restricting certain development activities without regulatory approval.

However, on 3 October 2025, the NRBT announced that the Supreme Court had dismissed the judicial review challenge brought by Tuita and Vea and dissolved the injunction that had prevented action against the former chief executive.

The Reserve Bank described the outcome as important for maintaining prudent banking management and financial stability.

Government-commissioned ADB investigation

The latest Vavaʻu allegations have also renewed questions about the findings of an Asian Development Bank (ADB) assessment commissioned by the government in 2025 following concerns about TDB’s lending practices and possible breaches of banking regulations.

In May 2025, Deputy Prime Minister Taniela Fusimālohi confirmed that the government had requested an external investigation after allegations emerged that TDB had breached lending rules, including restrictions on loans to individual borrowers.

The investigation followed criticism of a TOP$14 million lending scheme intended to assist low-income Tongans, including fishermen and weavers, amid allegations that some loans had instead benefited people with higher incomes. The bank’s then chief executive, ʻEmeline Tuita, denied those allegations.

In July 2025, Fusimālohi announced that the ADB assessment had been completed and submitted, with TDB’s newly appointed board beginning to act on its recommendations.

However, he declined to disclose the findings, leaving unanswered questions about the extent of any financial or regulatory breaches identified and the corrective measures recommended.

The previously undisclosed findings have gained renewed relevance following the latest police investigation involving TDB’s Vavaʻu branch, although no connection between the two matters has been established.
